questions.title: Why is the model called "1.58 bits" when weights can take 3 values {-1, 0, 1}?
questions.question_body: The paper introduces "BitNet b1.58" where every parameter is ternary, taking values in \{-1, 0, 1\}. The name suggests 1.58 bits per weight. I understand ternary values mean 3 possible states, and $\log_2(3) \approx 1.585$, so I assume this is where 1.58 comes from. But I'm confused: if each weight is stored as a ternary value, doesn't that still require 2 bits in practice (since you can't store 1.58 bits in hardware)? Is the 1.58 just a theoretical information-theoretic measure, or is there an actual encoding scheme that achieves this? And if it's theoretical, why not just call it a "ternary" or "2-bit" model?

questions.title: How can matrix multiplication use only integer addition and no multiplication?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that BitNet b1.58's matrix multiplication "only involves integer addition" and "requires almost no multiplication operations." I understand that if weights are in \{-1, 0, 1\}, then multiplying an activation by a weight is trivial: the result is either the activation, its negation, or zero. But the activations themselves are 8-bit integers, not ternary. So during matrix multiplication $\widetilde{W}x$, are we computing something like: for each row of $\widetilde{W}$, we sum the activations (or their negations) where the corresponding weight is +1 or -1, skipping where it's 0? Is this what they mean by "only addition"? And is this truly multiplication-free, or are there still some multiplications happening elsewhere?

questions.title: Why does adding 0 to the weight set enable "feature filtering"?
questions.question_body: The paper states that including 0 in the model weights (going from the original BitNet's \{-1, 1\} to \{-1, 0, 1\}) provides "explicit support for feature filtering, which can significantly improve the performance of 1-bit LLMs." I understand that a weight of 0 means a particular feature has no contribution to the output. But isn't a near-zero weight in a continuous-valued model effectively doing the same thing? Why is having an explicit 0 value qualitatively different from having a small floating-point weight? Is the claim that the ternary representation creates a form of structured sparsity that helps the model learn to ignore irrelevant features more effectively? Could someone elaborate on the mechanism by which this "feature filtering" improves performance?

questions.title: Is BitNet b1.58 a form of post-training quantization, and if not, why does it matter?
questions.question_body: The paper distinguishes BitNet b1.58 from post-training quantization methods like GPTQ and AWQ, stating that BitNet is "trained from scratch" with 1.58-bit weights. I'm confused about why training from scratch with quantized weights is better than quantizing after training. Intuitively, I would think a model trained with full precision would learn better representations, and then you could compress those representations afterward. Why does training with ternary weights from the start avoid the "sub-optimal" nature of post-training quantization that the paper mentions? Does the model learn fundamentally different representations when constrained to \{-1, 0, 1\} from the beginning?

questions.title: Why are activations 8-bit if this is a "1-bit" LLM?
questions.question_body: The paper describes BitNet b1.58 as having "1.58-bit weights and 8-bit activations." I'm confused about the asymmetry here. The title and framing emphasize the 1.58-bit nature, but the activations seem to be quantized to 8 bits, which is much higher. Why can't the activations also be ternary? Is there a fundamental reason why weights can be aggressively quantized but activations cannot? Does the 8-bit activation quantization limit the efficiency gains, or is the weight quantization the dominant factor in the memory and energy savings reported?

questions.title: Why does BitNet b1.58 only match FP16 LLaMA starting at 3B parameters?
questions.question_body: The results show that BitNet b1.58 matches the perplexity and zero-shot performance of FP16 LLaMA only starting from a 3B model size. For smaller models, there appears to be a performance gap. I'm wondering what causes this threshold. Is there something fundamental about model capacity that makes ternary weights insufficient for small models but adequate for larger ones? The paper mentions a "new scaling law" — does this imply that 1.58-bit models scale more favorably than FP16 models as size increases? If so, what is the theoretical explanation for why having fewer bits per weight hurts less at larger scales?

questions.title: How does the absmean quantization function work during backpropagation?
questions.question_body: The paper defines the absmean quantization function as $\widetilde{W} = \mathrm{RoundClip}(\frac{W}{\gamma + \epsilon}, -1, 1)$ where $\gamma = \frac{1}{nm}\sum_{ij}|W_{ij}|$. I understand the forward pass: you scale the weights by their mean absolute value, round to the nearest integer in \{-1, 0, 1\}, and clip. But I'm confused about how gradients flow through this during backpropagation. The round function is non-differentiable, and clipping has zero gradient outside the range. Does the paper use a straight-through estimator (STE) like in the original BitNet? If so, how does this interact with the absmean scaling factor $\gamma$, which itself depends on the weights? Does $\gamma$ get treated as a constant during backprop, or are gradients computed through it as well?

questions.title: What does "zero-point quantization" mean and why was it removed for activations?
questions.question_body: The paper states that for activation quantization, unlike the original BitNet, they "do not scale the activations before the non-linear functions to the range $[0, Q_b]$. Instead, the activations are all scaled to $[-Q_b, Q_b]$ per token to get rid of the zero-point quantization." I'm not familiar with zero-point quantization. What is it, and why does scaling to $[-Q_b, Q_b]$ instead of $[0, Q_b]$ eliminate it? The paper says this is "more convenient and simple for both implementation and system-level optimization, while introduces negligible effects to the performance." Could someone explain the trade-off here and why this change was made?

questions.title: Are the claimed efficiency equivalences (e.g., 13B BitNet vs 3B FP16) based on real measurements or extrapolation?
questions.question_body: The paper claims equivalences like "13B BitNet b1.58 is more efficient, in terms of latency, memory usage and energy consumption, than 3B FP16 LLM" and similar statements for other size pairs. I'm trying to understand whether these are direct measurements or extrapolations. The paper mentions evaluating models at 7B, 13B, and 70B sizes and reporting trends in Figure 1 and 2. Were these specific cross-size comparisons (e.g., 13B ternary vs 3B FP16) actually measured, or are they inferred from the trend lines? Also, does the memory comparison account for the embedding layer, which the paper notes "remains full precision"?

questions.title: Why does BitNet b1.58 use LLaMA-alike components, and does this affect the fairness of comparison?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that BitNet b1.58 adopts LLaMA-alike components (RMSNorm, SwiGLU, rotary embedding, no biases) and compares against a "reproduced FP16 LLaMA LLM." I'm wondering: was the original BitNet architecture different from LLaMA, and if so, does adopting LLaMA components conflate the architectural improvements with the quantization benefits? If the FP16 baseline is also LLaMA-based, then the comparison seems fair for isolating the effect of 1.58-bit quantization. But is there any possibility that some of the performance gains come from the architectural choices rather than the ternary weights? Also, is the "reproduced FP16 LLaMA" a well-validated baseline, or could there be training inefficiencies in the reproduction that make it an unfairly weak baseline?
